cmr.keyTitle: What is decided on day one
cmr.keyLead: Two things have to be established before the first letter goes out: how long the claim can still be brought, and which law governs it. Both answers follow from the CMR Convention, published in the Slovak Republic as Decree of the Minister of Foreign Affairs No. 11/1975 Coll. Under its Article 1(1) the Convention applies to every contract for the carriage of goods by road in vehicles for reward where the place of taking over of the goods and the place designated for delivery, as set out in the contract, are situated in two different countries, of which at least one is a contracting country — irrespective of the place of residence and the nationality of the parties.

key.title: Limitation under Article 32 CMR
key.desc: Under Article 32(1) of the Convention, the period of limitation for an action arising out of carriage under the Convention is one year; in the case of wilful misconduct, or such default as is considered equivalent to wilful misconduct by the law of the court seised of the case, the period is three years. A claim for payment of the carriage charges is not a claim for loss, damage or delay, so the residual category in Article 32(1)(c) comes into play: time runs from the expiry of three months after the making of the contract of carriage, and the day on which the period starts is not included in it. In practice the claim may be time-barred roughly fifteen months after the contract of carriage was concluded — from the conclusion of the contract, not from the invoice due date. Under Article 32(2) of the Convention, a written claim suspends the running of the limitation period until the day on which the carrier rejects the claim in writing and returns the documents attached to it; a further claim in the same matter does not suspend it again. That provision is framed around a claim rejected by the carrier — a letter before action by which the carrier itself pursues the carriage charges against the customer does not fall within its wording and does not suspend time. Apart from the case under paragraph 2, Article 32(3) provides that suspension and interruption of the limitation period are governed by the law of the court seised of the case; before a Slovak court that means Section 402 of the Commercial Code, under which time stops running only upon an act treated as the commencement of court proceedings or as the assertion of the right in proceedings already commenced. Reminders sent to the debtor do not extend the period.
key.note: Whether a carrier's claim for carriage charges is governed by the one-year period under Article 32 CMR or by the general four-year limitation period under Section 397 of the Slovak Commercial Code is not treated uniformly in professional practice. Given that uncertainty, it is appropriate to work with the shorter period.

key.title: Applicable law under the Rome I Regulation
key.desc: Where the parties have not chosen the applicable law, it is determined under Article 5(1) of Regulation (EC) No 593/2008 (Rome I): the law of the country of the carrier's habitual residence applies, provided that the place of receipt or the place of delivery or the consignor's habitual residence is also situated in that country. If those requirements are not met, the law of the country where the place of delivery as agreed by the parties is situated applies. Under Article 5(3), the law of another country applies where it is clear from all the circumstances of the case that the contract, in the absence of a choice of law, is manifestly more closely connected with that other country; the rule therefore does not displace a valid choice of law under Article 3.
key.note: The CMR Convention takes precedence to the extent that it governs the matter — this follows from Section 756 of the Slovak Commercial Code. Article 25(1) of the Rome I Regulation also provides that the Regulation does not prejudice the application of international conventions to which Member States are parties and which lay down conflict-of-law rules relating to contractual obligations. The law determined under the Regulation therefore applies only to questions the Convention does not govern; the carrier's claim for carriage charges is one of them.

key.title: Where the action can be brought — Article 31 CMR
key.desc: Under Article 31(1) of the Convention the claimant may bring an action in the courts of a contracting country designated by agreement between the parties, in the courts of the country in which the defendant is ordinarily resident or has his principal place of business or the branch or agency through which the contract of carriage was made, or in the courts of the country where the place of taking over of the goods or the place designated for delivery is situated; no other courts may be seised. Where the debtor is established in the Slovak Republic, or the goods were unloaded here, the Slovak courts have jurisdiction.
key.note: Under Article 71(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012 (Brussels I bis) the Regulation does not affect conventions which, in relation to particular matters, govern jurisdiction or the recognition and enforcement of judgments; under Article 71(2)(b) a judgment given in the exercise of jurisdiction provided for in such a convention is recognised and enforced in the other Member States in accordance with that Regulation. Where the convention itself lays down conditions for recognition or enforcement — Article 31(3) of the CMR Convention makes enforceability in the other contracting countries subject to the formalities prescribed there — those conditions apply; in any event, the provisions of the Regulation on recognition and enforcement, and therefore enforcement without a declaration of enforceability, may be applied.

steps.title: Taking the file on and analysing it
steps.desc: We take over the transport order, the CMR consignment note and the invoice. We verify whether the matter is governed by the CMR Convention, how long the claim can still be brought and what exactly makes up the principal sum.

steps.title: Checking the debtor
steps.desc: We check the commercial register, published financial statements, pending enforcement proceedings, and bankruptcy and restructuring proceedings. That shows whether proceedings are worth bringing and in what order to proceed.

steps.title: Letter before action
steps.desc: We prepare and send a demand for payment quantifying the principal, default interest and the flat-rate compensation for recovery costs. The demand also forms the basis for the steps that follow.

steps.title: Slovak payment order proceedings
steps.desc: If the debtor does not pay, we file an application under Act No. 307/2016 Coll. The application is filed exclusively by electronic means and the District Court Banská Bystrica has exclusive subject-matter jurisdiction. Where the payment order would have to be served on the defendant abroad, this route is not available (Section 3(6)(d) of the Act) — the European order for payment under Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006 then comes into play. Nor is the application admissible where the default interest claimed under the contract exceeds by more than five percentage points the rate that would apply without such an agreement (Section 3(5)(a) of the Act).

steps.title: Payment order or statement of opposition
steps.desc: The court issues the payment order no later than ten working days after the procedural conditions, including payment of the court fee, are met. From service of the payment order the defendant then has 15 days either to pay or to file a statement of opposition, which must be reasoned on the merits. If none is filed, the payment order has the effects of a final judgment; if one is filed, we respond to it and, within the 15-day period, apply for the proceedings to continue before the court having jurisdiction under the Civil Contentious Procedure Code.

steps.title: Enforcement
steps.desc: Once the decision is final and enforceable, we file an application for enforcement. The District Court Banská Bystrica has exclusive jurisdiction over enforcement proceedings and assigns the case to an enforcement officer at random — the creditor does not choose the officer. Where enforcement is already under way against the same debtor and the court has issued an authorisation to an officer, Section 55(4) of the Enforcement Code assigns every further case against that debtor to that same officer, and the random selection is not used.

steps.title: Escalation — bankruptcy
steps.desc: Where it turns out that the debtor is failing to pay several creditors, a bankruptcy petition and a claim against the statutory body for damage caused by failing to file in time come into consideration. We assess every such step separately: under Section 11(4) of Act No. 7/2005 Coll. a creditor is liable to the debtor and to other persons for damage arising from the effects of the commencement of bankruptcy proceedings if the court discontinues proceedings commenced on the creditor's petition because the debtor's solvency has been established, unless the creditor proves that it acted with professional care in filing the petition. A bankruptcy petition is therefore not a pressure tactic.

The court does not call on the applicant to pay it, and if the fee is not paid within 15 days of filing, the application is disregarded. The court fee for an application for enforcement is 25 euros under item 13(a) of the schedule. faq.q: How long do we have to bring a claim for unpaid carriage charges?
faq.a: Under Article 32(1) of the CMR Convention the basic period of limitation is one year. For a claim for payment of the carriage charges, point (c) applies: time runs from the expiry of three months after the making of the contract of carriage, and the day on which the period starts is not included in it. The claim may therefore be time-barred roughly fifteen months after the contract of carriage was concluded, not from the invoice due date. Whether this period or the general four-year period under Section 397 of the Slovak Commercial Code applies to carriage charges is not treated uniformly in professional practice, so it is appropriate to work with the shorter period. Under Article 32(2) of the Convention a written claim suspends time until the day the carrier rejects it in writing and returns the documents attached to it; a letter before action by which the carrier itself pursues the carriage charges does not fall within that provision and does not suspend time — before a Slovak court, time stops running under Section 402 of the Commercial Code only when the right is asserted in court. Under Article 32(4) of the Convention, a time-barred claim may not be made the subject of a counter-claim or set-off.

faq.q: Can we sue a Slovak customer in Slovakia?
faq.a: Under Article 31(1) of the CMR Convention the claimant may bring an action, among other options, in the courts of the country in which the defendant has his principal place of business, and in the courts of the country where the place of taking over of the goods or the place designated for delivery is situated; no other courts may be seised. Where the debtor is established in the Slovak Republic, or the goods were unloaded here, the Slovak courts have jurisdiction. Under Article 31(5) of the Convention, no security for costs of proceedings may be required from nationals of contracting countries resident or having their place of business in one of those countries.

faq.q: Which law governs the matter if we did not choose one?
faq.a: The CMR Convention takes precedence to the extent that it governs the matter; this follows from Section 756 of the Slovak Commercial Code, and Article 25(1) of the Rome I Regulation leaves the application of such conventions unaffected. Questions the Convention does not govern — including the claim for payment of the carriage charges itself — are governed by the law determined under Article 5(1) of the Rome I Regulation: the law of the country of habitual residence of the carrier, provided the place of receipt or the place of delivery or the habitual residence of the consignor is also situated in that country; failing that, the law of the country of the agreed place of delivery.

faq.q: Can we claim interest and costs on top of the principal?
faq.a: Under Section 369(1) of the Slovak Commercial Code a creditor which has performed its own statutory and contractual obligations has the right to default interest without any separate reminder. Where the rate was not agreed, Section 369(2) of the Commercial Code applies the rate laid down by Government Regulation No. 21/2013 Coll.: under Section 1(1) the base interest rate of the European Central Bank in force on the first day of the relevant calendar half-year of default, increased by eight percentage points, or — if the creditor opts for the fixed variant under Section 1(2) — the base rate in force on the first day of default increased by nine percentage points. The current ECB base rate has to be checked as at the relevant date. Alongside interest, Section 369c(1) of the Commercial Code gives the creditor the right to flat-rate compensation for the costs of recovering the claim; under Section 2 of Government Regulation No. 21/2013 Coll. that is 40 euros, once, regardless of how long the default lasts.

faq.q: How quickly does the court decide, and what happens if the debtor opposes?
faq.a: In payment order proceedings under Act No. 307/2016 Coll. the court issues the payment order no later than ten working days after the procedural conditions, including payment of the court fee, are met. From service of the payment order the defendant has 15 days to pay or to file a statement of opposition, which must be reasoned on the merits; opposition without reasons on the merits is rejected by the court. If no opposition is filed, the payment order has the effects of a final judgment. If opposition is filed, it has to be answered within 15 days and, within the same period, an application made for the proceedings to continue before the court having jurisdiction under the Civil Contentious Procedure Code — otherwise the proceedings are discontinued.

faq.q: What if the debtor has no assets?
faq.a: Enforcement is carried out by an enforcement officer appointed by the District Court Banská Bystrica at random; the creditor does not choose the officer. Where the debtor has been in default for more than 90 days on at least two monetary obligations owed to more than one creditor and has been called on in writing by one of those creditors to pay, its insolvency may reasonably be presumed under Section 11(3) of Act No. 7/2005 Coll. and a bankruptcy petition may be filed. Under Section 11a(1) of the same Act, the person obliged to file a bankruptcy petition on the debtor's behalf is liable for damage caused to the debtor's creditors by failing to file in time; under Section 11a(3), unless a different amount is proven, the damage is presumed to be the amount of the creditor's claim that went unsatisfied after the bankruptcy proceedings were discontinued for want of assets, after the bankruptcy was cancelled for want of assets, or after enforcement against the debtor was terminated for want of assets. Under Section 11a(4), the creditor's claims arising from that liability become time-barred no earlier than one year after the bankruptcy proceedings were discontinued for want of assets, after the bankruptcy was cancelled for want of assets, or after enforcement against the debtor was terminated for want of assets.

cfr.keyLead: All three tracks run under the same Act on the Residence of Aliens, but the conditions, the evidence required and the length of the permit differ sharply between them.

key.title: Temporary residence for business purposes
key.desc: Under Section 22(1) of Act No. 404/2011 Coll. on the Residence of Aliens, this permit is granted to a third-country national who carries on or will carry on business in Slovakia as a self-employed person (point (a)), or who acts or will act on behalf of a trading company or cooperative without being in an employment relationship with it (point (b)) — in practice, its director. Since 1 July 2025 it is granted for a fixed three years (Section 22(2)), not for the expected duration of the activity. Alongside it you must show financial security for the business activity in a dedicated business account: one hundred times the subsistence minimum for a director, twenty times for a self-employed person, and forty times for a director whose business plan has been assessed as an innovative project (Section 32(7)). Financial security for the residence itself is a further twelve times the subsistence minimum (Section 32(14)).
key.note: The renewal test changed on 15 July 2026 (amending Act No. 128/2026 Coll.). For a director, the company's after-tax profit is no longer assessed; what counts is tax actually paid, at least at the level of the minimum corporate tax under Section 46b(2) of the Income Tax Act (Section 34(6)). A self-employed applicant instead shows taxable income above the threshold in Section 32(1) of the Income Tax Act (Section 34(5)). Older sources still quote twenty or sixty times the subsistence minimum — that is the position up to 14 July 2026. Plan the company's first tax return around the new test, not the renewal application.

key.title: EU Blue Card
key.desc: The Blue Card is governed by Sections 37 to 41 of the Act, transposing Directive (EU) 2021/1883. Under Section 37(3) it covers employment requiring higher professional qualifications and carrying a monthly salary of at least 1.2 times the average monthly wage of an employee in the Slovak economy for the calendar year preceding the year of application; where the applicant obtained their degree no more than three years before applying, the plain average wage is enough. Qualification is proved by a decision recognising the university degree — or, for the occupations listed in Annex 3 to the Act (ICT managers and specialists), by evidence of higher professional skills acquired over at least three years within the seven years preceding the application (Section 37(5)).
key.note: The police authority decides within 30 days of receiving a complete application (Section 38(7)) — against 60 days for standard employment residence. The employment relationship must be agreed for at least six months; that condition sits not in the Residence of Aliens Act but in Section 21a(4)(d) of Act No. 5/2004 Coll. on Employment Services. The Blue Card also carries EU-wide labour mobility and a shorter path to permanent residence — worth checking even where a standard work permit would also be available.

key.title: Temporary residence for employment
key.desc: Section 23 of the Act covers the standard route: the employer first reports the vacancy, the labour office issues a confirmation that it can be filled, and only then does the police authority decide on residence. The permit is granted for the expected duration of the employment, up to five years (Section 23(3)). For an intra-company transfer it is up to three years for a manager or specialist and up to one year for a trainee employee (Section 23(5)). Seasonal employment is capped at 240 days within any 12 consecutive months (Section 23(4)).
key.note: The police authority decides within 60 days of receiving a complete application (Section 33(8)(b)); where the role is one with a recognised labour shortage in the region, the deadline is 30 days (Section 33(8)(c)). That decision is preceded by reporting the vacancy and obtaining the labour office's confirmation, so plan the overall timeline in months rather than weeks — and obtain the supporting documents late enough that they are still valid when the application is filed.

cfr.stepsTitle: How the two matters run together

steps.title: Assessment
steps.desc: We establish which of the three tracks fits your situation, what the Slovak company structure needs to look like, and what evidence each authority will ask for.

steps.title: Company formation
steps.desc: Where a company does not exist yet, we draft the founder’s deed or memorandum of association and authorise it as attorneys — since 17 August 2026 that is, alongside a notarial deed, the only permitted form (Section 57 of the Commercial Code). You do not need to be in Slovakia to sign: a representative signs for you under a power of attorney with an officially certified signature (Section 57(2)). We file the registration electronically; the registry court registers the company within two working days of receiving a complete application (Section 58(1) of Act No. 29/2026 Coll.).

steps.title: Residence application
steps.desc: We prepare the application file, including confirmations from the company, and file it with the foreign police. Where required, we guide you through certifying documents abroad or obtaining an apostille.

steps.title: Decision and registration
steps.desc: Once residence is granted, we handle what follows on the company side — the business bank account, tax registration and, where relevant, the registered seat.

steps.title: Renewal
steps.desc: We track the renewal deadlines and the evidence each track requires — taxable income, tax paid or the Blue Card salary threshold — so the permit does not lapse.

cfr.docsLead: The exact list depends on which track applies; these five cover most matters at the outset.
docs: Valid travel document, valid for at least six months beyond the intended stay.
Extract from the criminal record of your home country (and of any country of residence in the last three years), apostilled or otherwise legalised where required — not older than 90 days at filing.
Proof of secured accommodation in Slovakia.

For the business track: extract from the Slovak commercial register (once the company is formed) or the draft incorporation documents; for remote formation, a power of attorney with an officially certified signature, apostilled or otherwise legalised where required.

For the employment tracks: the employment contract or the employer's written promise of employment, and — for the Blue Card — proof of qualification: the decision recognising the university degree, or evidence of higher professional skills for the ICT occupations listed in Annex 3 to the Act.
cfr.priceLead: The scope and the fee are agreed in advance and in writing, for each part of the matter separately.

price.label: Company formation
price.desc: Full formation including attorney authorisation of the founding documents, filing with the commercial register and arranging the trade licences — the same fee we quote for any Slovak s.r.o. The EUR 220 court fee for first registration is paid separately.

price.desc: Assessing which track applies, preparing the application and representing you before the foreign police. Quoted once we know which of the three tracks fits your matter.

price.desc: Court and administrative fees, sworn translations where required, and the registered seat, if you use one — see below.

Where you need one of these, we point you to an independently licensed provider, and their invoice is separate from ours — never bundled into our fee. This keeps each service under the licence that actually covers it, and keeps our advice to you free of any referral interest.
cfr.formLead: Tell us whether you already have a Slovak company, what your role in it is or will be, and where you are applying from. We will get back to you and set out which track applies. Submitting this form does not create a lawyer-client relationship.

faq.q: Can I own a Slovak company without living in Slovakia?
faq.a: Yes. Owning a share carries no residence condition for anyone — for the founder and shareholder of an s.r.o. the registry court checks tax and enforcement obstacles, not residence. The residence condition attaches to the person authorised to act on behalf of the company, typically the director: under Section 51(4) of Act No. 29/2026 Coll. on the Commercial Register the registry court checks, before registration, whether that person holds a Slovak residence permit, unless they are a national of an EU member state, an EEA state or an OECD state. The permit itself is then obtained as temporary residence for business purposes under Section 22 of Act No. 404/2011 Coll. A shareholder who is not a director needs no permit at all. Note that this is a condition for entry in the commercial register; for skilled and regulated trades the responsible representative must additionally be resident in Slovakia or otherwise authorised to reside here (Section 11(3) of the Trade Licensing Act) — a separate condition.

faq.q: Do I have to go to a notary to form the company?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Since 17 August 2026 the memorandum of association and the founder’s deed must be drawn up either as a notarial deed or as a document authorised by an attorney (Section 57(1) and (3) of the Commercial Code as amended by Act No. 29/2026 Coll.). Authorisation means the attorney draws up the document, verifies the identity of the party and any representative and assesses the act’s compliance with the law (Section 1a(2) of Act No. 586/2003 Coll. on the Legal Profession); the document is deposited the same day in the Slovak Bar Association’s register of authorisations. Where a document is authorised by an attorney, no official certification of signatures is required (Section 50(4) of Act No. 29/2026 Coll.). A notarial deed remains mandatory for later general-meeting decisions of a multi-member s.r.o. on managing directors or on changes to shares (Section 127a(4) of the Commercial Code).

faq.q: Do I need to found the company before I apply for residence, or the other way round?
faq.a: In practice the company has to exist, or at least be filed for registration, before the residence application can show what the director will be doing in Slovakia. We sequence the two so the residence file is ready to submit as soon as the company is registered, rather than waiting afterwards.

faq.q: What is the difference between the EU Blue Card and a standard work permit?
faq.a: Both authorise employment, but the Blue Card is reserved for roles meeting the qualification and salary conditions of Sections 37 ff. of Act No. 404/2011 Coll. (transposing Directive (EU) 2021/1883): a recognised university degree — or, for the ICT occupations listed in Annex 3 to the Act, three years' professional experience gained within the preceding seven — and a salary of at least 1.2 times the average monthly wage of an employee in the Slovak economy for the preceding calendar year, or the plain average wage for a graduate within three years of obtaining the degree. The employment relationship must be agreed for at least six months (Section 21a(4)(d) of Act No. 5/2004 Coll.). Where a role qualifies, the Blue Card is decided within 30 days against 60 for standard employment residence, and carries EU-wide mobility and an easier path to permanent residence.

faq.q: Can my family come with me?
faq.a: Family reunification is available under both the business and employment tracks and under the Blue Card, with the Blue Card route generally the most straightforward. We assess it alongside the main application, not as an afterthought.

faq.q: Do you handle accounting, the registered seat, a work permit for staff I hire, or finding accommodation?
faq.a: No, not under our own roof, and deliberately so. Each of those is a separately regulated activity — accounting requires its own registration, employment intermediation for payment requires a licence issued by the labour office under Act No. 5/2004 Coll., and a registered-seat provider carries its own disclosure and, since June 2026, goAML registration duties. We point you to a provider holding the relevant licence, who invoices you separately — we do not mark it up or take a referral fee.

faq.q: How long does the whole process take?
faq.a: Forming the company itself takes one to two weeks once the documents are signed. The residence decision is bound by statutory deadlines under Section 33(8) of Act No. 404/2011 Coll., and Section 38(7) for the Blue Card: 30 days for the Blue Card, 60 days for employment-based residence, and 90 days for the remaining purposes including business. Those periods start only once the application is complete, and obtaining documents from abroad comes first. We therefore recommend starting three to four months before the date you need to be operating in Slovakia.

xdr.metaTitle: Recovering a debt from a Slovak company
xdr.metaDescription: Slovak customer not paying for goods, services or subcontract work? Jurisdiction, applicable law, payment order proceedings, enforcement. Law firm in Zvolen.
xdr.heroTitle: Recovering a debt from a Slovak company
xdr.heroLead: A customer established in the Slovak Republic has not paid an invoice for goods, services or subcontract work. We establish in which court and under which law the claim can be brought, check the debtor in the public registers and run the matter from the letter before action through to enforcement.
heroPara: We act for foreign companies — suppliers of goods, service providers, construction and installation companies, and creditors under loans between companies — whose debtor is established in Slovakia. We advise exclusively on the law of the Slovak Republic; where your contract is governed by the law of another state, we work alongside your local counsel there.
We work in English and Slovak and can run the whole matter remotely.
xdr.whoLead: We focus on monetary claims of foreign businesses against debtors established in the Slovak Republic — whatever the sector. Carriage charges under the CMR Convention have a page of their own; this one covers goods, services, construction and installation subcontracts, and loans between companies.

who.title: Suppliers of goods
who.desc: Unpaid invoices for goods delivered — including cases where the customer never disputed the invoice and simply does not pay, and cases where it began to allege defects only after the demand for payment.

who.title: Service and IT providers
who.desc: Fees for services rendered, software development and licences, maintenance or equipment rental. We assess what you can use to prove that you performed — acceptance protocols, work reports, e-mail confirmations.

who.title: Construction and installation companies
who.desc: Subcontracts on construction sites in Slovakia and installation of technology: unpaid interim invoices, retained parts of the price and unsigned handover protocols. We check your direct contractual partner in the subcontracting chain, because the claim lies against that partner.

who.title: Creditors under loans between companies
who.desc: Unrepaid loans and credit granted to a Slovak company — a business partner or a group company. We assess the contract, the proof that the money was advanced and the due date, and check whether the debtor has meanwhile entered bankruptcy or restructuring.

xdr.keyTitle: What you need to know before the first step
xdr.keyLead: With a cross-border claim, three questions are decided first: which court has jurisdiction, which law governs the contract, and whether recovery against the particular debtor makes economic sense. Jurisdiction and the applicable law are determined by directly applicable regulations of the European Union; the procedure before a Slovak court and enforcement are governed by Slovak law.

key.title: Where to sue — jurisdiction of the Slovak courts
key.desc: The rules are laid down by Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council (Brussels I bis). Under Article 4(1), persons domiciled in a Member State are to be sued in the courts of that Member State; under Article 63(1), a company is domiciled at the place where it has its statutory seat, central administration or principal place of business. A debtor established in the Slovak Republic can therefore be sued in a Slovak court, unless the parties have agreed on the jurisdiction of another court. In addition, Article 7(1) allows, in matters relating to a contract, an action in the courts for the place of performance of the obligation: unless otherwise agreed, that is, in the case of the sale of goods, the place in a Member State where, under the contract, the goods were delivered or should have been delivered, and, in the case of the provision of services, the place in a Member State where, under the contract, the services were provided or should have been provided. A creditor may therefore sometimes choose between a court in its own state and a Slovak court. A decision of a Slovak court is directly a basis for enforcement in Slovakia — that is, in the state where the debtor is established.
key.note: A jurisdiction clause in the contract or in the general terms and conditions: under Article 25(1) of the Regulation, the court of a Member State on which the parties have agreed has jurisdiction, and that jurisdiction is exclusive unless the parties have agreed otherwise. The agreement must be in writing or evidenced in writing, in a form which accords with practices which the parties have established between themselves, or — in international trade or commerce — in a form which accords with a usage of which the parties are or ought to have been aware; under Article 25(2), any communication by electronic means which provides a durable record of the agreement is also treated as being in writing. Where the contract, or terms and conditions that have become part of it, designate a court of another Member State, the action belongs before that court; under Article 26(1), however, a court before which the defendant enters an appearance without contesting jurisdiction also has jurisdiction. We therefore read the jurisdiction clause first.

key.title: Which law governs the contract — the Rome I Regulation
key.desc: The jurisdiction of the court and the applicable law are two separate questions: a Slovak court may decide under the law of another state. Under Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 593/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council (Rome I), a contract is governed by the law chosen by the parties; the choice must be made expressly or clearly demonstrated by the terms of the contract or the circumstances of the case. Where the parties have not chosen the law, under Article 4(1) a contract for the sale of goods is governed by the law of the country where the seller has its habitual residence (point (a)) and a contract for the provision of services by the law of the country where the service provider has its habitual residence (point (b)); a contract not covered by paragraph 1 is governed, under Article 4(2), by the law of the country where the party required to effect the characteristic performance of the contract has its habitual residence. Under Article 19(1), the habitual residence of a company is the place of its central administration. For a foreign supplier that generally means the law of its own state, not Slovak law — unless it is clear from all the circumstances of the case that the contract is manifestly more closely connected with another country (Article 4(3)). Under Article 12(1), the applicable law governs in particular the performance of contractual obligations, the consequences of their breach, and also prescription and limitation of actions (point (d)). The length of the limitation period and the right to default interest may therefore be governed by the law of your state even though the action is brought in Slovakia.
key.note: In a sale of goods between businesses from different states, the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods (CISG) may also come into play, if the conditions for its application are met and the parties have not excluded it. A Slovak court ascertains the content of foreign law under Section 53(1) of Act No. 97/1963 Coll. on private international law and procedure: it takes all necessary measures, including ascertaining the content of the foreign law by its own means, from generally available sources, by imposing a duty on the parties to the proceedings or by requesting information from the Ministry of Justice of the Slovak Republic; if the content of the foreign law cannot be ascertained within a reasonable time, Slovak law applies. Our firm advises exclusively on the law of the Slovak Republic — questions of the substantive law of another state we handle in cooperation with your local counsel there.

key.title: Where Slovak law governs the relationship: limitation and acknowledgement of the obligation
key.desc: Slovak law governs the contract in particular where the parties have chosen it or where that follows from Article 4 of the Rome I Regulation. Obligations between entrepreneurs that relate to their business activity are then governed by the Slovak Commercial Code (Section 261(1)). Under Section 397 the limitation period is four years, unless the law provides otherwise for particular rights. Under Section 402 it stops running only when the creditor performs a legal act which, under the rules governing court proceedings, is treated as the commencement of court proceedings or as the assertion of the right in proceedings already commenced — reminders and demands for payment do not in themselves stop the limitation period running. If the debtor acknowledges its obligation in writing, a new four-year limitation period runs from that acknowledgement under Section 407(1), even where the right was already time-barred at the time of the acknowledgement (Section 407(4)). Payment of interest is also treated as acknowledgement in respect of the sum on which the interest is paid (Section 407(2)), as is part performance, if it can be inferred that by it the debtor also acknowledges the remainder of the obligation (Section 407(3)). Where a person acknowledges a specific obligation in writing, it is presumed under Section 323(1) that the obligation exists, to the acknowledged extent, at the time of the acknowledgement. A written acknowledgement of the debt is therefore the first thing we ask the debtor for when negotiating instalments.
key.note: Under Section 408(1) of the Commercial Code, the limitation period ends, irrespective of other provisions, no later than ten years from the day on which it first began to run. Where the contract is governed by the law of another state, these periods do not apply — limitation is assessed under the applicable law (Article 12(1)(d) of the Rome I Regulation). With an older claim, the first step is therefore to determine the applicable law, not to count four years.

key.title: Default interest and the 40-euro flat-rate compensation under Slovak law
key.desc: Where Slovak law governs the relationship, the debtor of a monetary obligation is in default under Section 365(2) of the Commercial Code if it does not perform properly and no later than within 30 days of the date of receipt of the invoice or another demand for payment, or within 30 days of the date on which the creditor performed, whichever of those days is later — unless a different payment period follows from the contract. Under Section 369(1), a creditor which has performed its own statutory and contractual obligations has the right to default interest at the rate agreed in the contract, without any separate reminder. Where no rate was agreed, Section 369(2) applies the rate laid down by Government Regulation of the Slovak Republic No. 21/2013 Coll.: under Section 1(1) the base interest rate of the European Central Bank in force on the first day of the relevant calendar half-year of default, increased by eight percentage points, or — if the creditor opts for the fixed variant under Section 1(2) — the base rate in force on the first day of default increased by nine percentage points, which then applies throughout the period of default. Alongside interest, Section 369c(1) of the Commercial Code gives the creditor the right to flat-rate compensation for the costs of recovering the claim; under Section 2 of the Government Regulation that is 40 euros, once, regardless of how long the default lasts.
key.note: The current base interest rate of the European Central Bank has to be checked as at the relevant date. A restriction applies to Slovak payment order proceedings: the application is not admissible where agreed default interest is claimed at a rate exceeding by more than five percentage points the rate that would apply without such an agreement (Section 3(5)(a) of Act No. 307/2016 Coll.). Where the contract is governed by the law of another state, default interest and compensation for recovery costs are assessed under that law.

key.title: Slovak payment order proceedings or the European order for payment
key.desc: Slovak payment order proceedings (upomínacie konanie) under Act No. 307/2016 Coll. are accelerated electronic proceedings for monetary claims, an alternative to an action under the Civil Contentious Procedure Code (Section 1(2)). The District Court Banská Bystrica has exclusive subject-matter jurisdiction (Section 2). The application is filed exclusively by electronic means using the designated form (Section 4(1)), and the claimant — or, if represented, its representative — must have an activated electronic mailbox (elektronická schránka) set up under the Slovak e-Government Act (Section 3(6)(b)); a foreign creditor therefore generally files the application through a Slovak lawyer. A foreign legal person proves its identification details by an extract from the register in which it is entered (Section 4(3)). Only a claim for payment of a sum of money in euros can be asserted (Section 3(2)). The application is not admissible if the payment order would have to be served on the defendant abroad (Section 3(6)(d)) — this restriction concerns the defendant, not the claimant, so the fact that the creditor is established abroad is no obstacle. The court issues the payment order no later than ten working days after the procedural conditions, including payment of the court fee, are met (Section 7(1)). The defendant has 15 days from service either to pay or to file a statement of opposition (odpor) (Section 7(2)), which must be reasoned on the merits (Section 11(1)); a payment order against which no statement of opposition has been filed has the effects of a final judgment (Section 11(6)). The European order for payment under Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006 is intended for cross-border cases — that is, cases in which at least one of the parties is domiciled or habitually resident in a Member State other than the Member State of the court seised (Article 3(1)). A foreign creditor suing a Slovak debtor in a Slovak court meets that condition. The application is made using standard form A (Article 7(1)), in Slovakia in the state language (Section 270 of the Civil Contentious Procedure Code). The court issues the order as soon as possible and normally within 30 days of the lodging of the application (Article 12(1)). The defendant may lodge a statement of opposition within 30 days of service and does not have to specify the reasons (Article 16(2) and (3)); the proceedings then continue before the competent court of the Member State of origin (Article 17(1)). An order which has become enforceable is recognised and enforced in the other Member States without the need for a declaration of enforceability (Article 19); the Regulation does not apply to Denmark (Article 2(3)).
key.note: For a claim in euros against a debtor established in Slovakia, Slovak payment order proceedings have, compared with the European order for payment, a shorter statutory period for issuing the order and half the court fee (Section 11c(1) of Act No. 71/1992 Coll.), and they require a statement of opposition reasoned on the merits. The European order for payment comes into play mainly where Slovak payment order proceedings are not admissible. For claims whose value, excluding interest, expenses and disbursements, does not exceed 5 000 euros, there is also the European Small Claims Procedure under Regulation (EC) No 861/2007 (Article 2(1)): it is a written procedure (Article 5(1)), it is commenced by standard claim Form A (Article 4(1)), the forms are submitted in the language in which the court conducts the proceedings (Article 6(1)), and the judgment is recognised and enforced in another Member State without the need for a declaration of enforceability (Article 20(1)).

key.title: A decision from another Member State and enforcement in Slovakia
key.desc: If you sued the debtor in your own state — for example on the basis of a jurisdiction clause or at the place of performance — and hold an enforceable decision, there is no need to sue again in Slovakia. Under Article 39 of Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012, a judgment given in a Member State which is enforceable in that Member State is enforceable in the other Member States without any declaration of enforceability being required. For the purposes of enforcement, Article 42(1) requires a copy of the judgment which satisfies the conditions necessary to establish its authenticity, and the certificate which the court of origin issues on request under Article 53. Under Article 43(1), the certificate is served on the person against whom enforcement is sought prior to the first enforcement measure. Under Article 41(1), enforcement is governed by the law of the Member State addressed — in Slovakia, therefore, by the Enforcement Code, under which a foreign enforcement title enforceable in the Slovak Republic is also an enforcement title (Section 45(2)(b)).
key.note: The enforcement authority may require a translation of the judgment only if it is unable to proceed without such a translation (Article 42(4) of the Brussels I bis Regulation); it may require a translation or a transliteration of the contents of the certificate where necessary (Article 42(3)). In Slovakia the District Court Banská Bystrica has exclusive subject-matter jurisdiction over enforcement proceedings (Section 49 of the Enforcement Code). The court fee for an application for enforcement is 25 euros under item 13(a) of the schedule of fees in Act No. 71/1992 Coll.

steps.title: Taking the file on and analysing it
steps.desc: We go through the contract, purchase orders, terms and conditions, invoices and proof of performance. We check whether the contract contains a jurisdiction clause or a choice-of-law clause, which court has jurisdiction, which law governs the relationship and until when the claim can be brought. The result is a written proposal of how to proceed.

steps.title: Checking the debtor
steps.desc: Before bringing an action we check the debtor in the public registers. The Commercial Register is a public list; the registered data and the documents filed in its collection of documents are published free of charge (Section 3(1) and Section 6(1) of Act No. 29/2026 Coll.). The Register of Financial Statements makes the documents filed in its public part available to everyone free of charge (Section 23c(1) of Act No. 431/2002 Coll.). The Slovak Insolvency Register records bankruptcy and restructuring proceedings (Section 203b of Act No. 7/2005 Coll.), and the Central Register of Enforcement Proceedings, kept by the Slovak Chamber of Enforcement Officers, is a public list of enforcement proceedings that have not been finally concluded (Section 211a of the Enforcement Code). The check shows whether recovery makes economic sense and whether the debtor is in bankruptcy or restructuring — in that case the claim is asserted not by an action but by lodging it in those proceedings (prihláška pohľadávky).

steps.title: Letter before action, acknowledgement of debt, instalments
steps.desc: We prepare and send a demand for payment quantifying the principal, default interest and other claims under the applicable law. If the debtor does not dispute the debt but cannot pay it at once, we agree a written acknowledgement of the obligation and an instalment schedule. The agreement can also be drawn up as a notarial deed: if it contains a legal obligation, identifies the entitled person and the obliged person, the legal basis, the subject matter and the time of performance, and the obliged person has consented in it to enforceability, it is an enforcement title under Section 45(2)(c) of the Enforcement Code. If the obligation is not performed, an application for enforcement can then be filed without prior court proceedings.

steps.title: Bringing the claim in court
steps.desc: If the debtor does not pay, we file an application in payment order proceedings under Act No. 307/2016 Coll. — exclusively by electronic means, with the District Court Banská Bystrica, which has exclusive subject-matter jurisdiction over these proceedings. The court issues the payment order no later than ten working days after the procedural conditions, including payment of the court fee, are met; from service the defendant has 15 days either to pay or to file a statement of opposition reasoned on the merits. If none is filed, the payment order has the effects of a final judgment. If one is filed, we respond to it and, within the 15-day period, apply for the proceedings to continue before the court having jurisdiction under the Civil Contentious Procedure Code (Section 14(1) of the Act). Where payment order proceedings are not admissible, we file an application for a European order for payment or bring an action.

steps.title: Enforcement
steps.desc: With an enforceable decision we file an application for enforcement — electronically, using the designated form (Section 48(7) of the Enforcement Code). The District Court Banská Bystrica has exclusive subject-matter jurisdiction over enforcement proceedings (Section 49). Unless there are grounds for dismissing the application, the court issues the authorisation to carry out enforcement within 15 days of receiving the application (Section 53(1); that period does not apply in the case of a notarial deed). It assigns the case to an enforcement officer at random (Section 55(1)) — the creditor does not choose the officer. Where enforcement is already under way against the same debtor and the court has issued an authorisation to an officer, Section 55(4) assigns every further case to that same officer.

xdr.docsLead: Send us the documents as scans or photographs in the language in which they were drawn up; neither originals nor translations are needed at this stage. We will determine what needs to be translated once we have assessed the matter.
docs: The contract, purchase orders and their confirmations, including the e-mail exchange under which the contract was concluded, and the general terms and conditions referred to — we look in them for a jurisdiction clause and a choice-of-law clause.
Invoices and proof that they were sent or delivered to the debtor.
Proof of performance: delivery notes and transport documents for the delivery of goods, handover and acceptance protocols, work reports, the site diary or installation reports.
For a loan or credit: the contract and proof that the money was advanced, for example a bank statement.
Correspondence with the debtor — reminders, complaints, notified set-offs and deductions, promises of payment, acknowledgements of debt, part payments.

A current extract from the register in which your company is entered; in payment order proceedings a foreign legal person uses it to prove its identification details (Section 4(3) of Act No. 307/2016 Coll.).
Details of the bank account to which the debtor is to pay; they are mandatory in an application for a payment order (Section 4(4) of Act No. 307/2016 Coll.).

Where a court decision from another Member State already exists: a copy of it and the certificate under Article 53 of Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012, or a European order for payment declared enforceable.
xdr.priceLead: The scope and the fee are agreed in advance and in writing. You know the price for the assessment and for the letter before action before we start work.

price.label: Assessment of the matter
price.desc: We go through the documents, check jurisdiction, the applicable law and limitation, check the debtor in the public registers and set out the procedure we propose. We quote the fee before any work starts; if you decide not to go ahead, the matter ends there.

price.label: Letter before action
price.desc: Preparing and sending the demand for payment, including the calculation of the principal and ancillary claims. Agreed as a fixed sum for the step, not at an hourly rate.

price.label: Representation in proceedings
price.desc: Under Section 7(1) of Decree of the Ministry of Justice of the Slovak Republic No. 655/2004 Coll., a contingency fee may be agreed in the form of a percentage share in the value of the matter; under Section 7(2) its maximum amount may not exceed 20 % of that value. Under Section 8(1) of the Decree it becomes payable only where the client has been fully successful in the matter; where the client is partly successful the lawyer is entitled under Section 8(2) to the tariff fee determined according to the degree of success, and where the client has not been successful even in part the lawyer may under Section 8(3) claim only reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses.

xdr.priceNote: Out-of-pocket expenses arise alongside the lawyer’s fee, in particular court fees and translation costs. In payment order proceedings the court fee is, under Section 11c(1) of Act No. 71/1992 Coll. on court fees, 50 % of the percentage rate set out in the schedule of fees; the basic rate under item 1(a) of the schedule is 6 % of the value of the subject matter, so 3 % in these proceedings, but not less than 25 euros and not more than 25 000 euros, or 50 000 euros in commercial matters. The court does not call on the applicant to pay it, and if the fee is not paid within 15 days of filing, the application is disregarded. For an application for a European order for payment, note 5 to item 1 of the schedule provides that the fee is payable under item 1(a), that is, 6 %. The court fee for an application for enforcement is 25 euros under item 13(a) of the schedule. The court awards a party its costs of the proceedings in proportion to its success in the matter (Section 255(1) of the Civil Contentious Procedure Code). The outcome of proceedings depends on the circumstances of the individual case, in particular on the debtor’s assets.
xdr.formTitle: Send us the papers on your claim
xdr.formLead: Tell us who the debtor is, what it owes you for, how much and since when. We will get back to you and set out the next steps. Submitting this form does not create a lawyer-client relationship.

faq.q: Do we have to come to Slovakia for the proceedings?
faq.a: In most matters, no. An application in payment order proceedings is filed exclusively by electronic means, and the claim asserted is assessed on the basis of the facts stated in the application and the documents attached to it (Section 3(3) and Section 4(1) of Act No. 307/2016 Coll.); an application for enforcement is likewise filed electronically (Section 48(7) of the Enforcement Code). Before the court a party may be represented by a representative of its choice (Section 89(1) of the Civil Contentious Procedure Code) — at hearings we represent you. If, following the debtor’s statement of opposition, the matter is heard in ordinary proceedings and the court orders the examination of a party, the parties are obliged to attend for examination (Section 195(2)); the court may, however, exceptionally and for reasons of procedural economy, order a party to answer the questions in writing (Section 195(3)), and where the physical presence of a party at the hearing is not required to guarantee a fair trial, it allows the party to take part by videoconference or other means of communication technology (Section 175(2)).

faq.q: The invoice is in another currency (for example Polish zloty) and the contract is in a foreign language — is that a problem?
faq.a: It is no obstacle to the claim, but it does affect the choice of procedure. Under Section 3(2) of Act No. 307/2016 Coll., Slovak payment order proceedings are intended for claims for payment of a specific sum of money in euros. A claim denominated in another currency is therefore pursued by an application for a European order for payment or by an action under the Civil Contentious Procedure Code; Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006 speaks of pecuniary claims for a specific amount and contains no restriction to the euro. In Slovakia an application for a European order for payment is filed in the state language, that is, in Slovak (Section 270 of the Civil Contentious Procedure Code); we draft all submissions on your behalf in Slovak. Where the contract, purchase orders and invoices are in a foreign language, expect them to need translating into Slovak — which documents to translate we determine when assessing the matter, so that no more is translated than necessary. Should you appear before the court in person, you have the right under Section 155(1) of the Civil Contentious Procedure Code to act in your mother tongue or in a language you understand; the court, having regard to the nature and circumstances of the matter, engages an interpreter, and the associated costs are borne by the state under Section 155(2).

faq.q: Our contract says nothing about the court or the applicable law. Where do we sue, and under which law?
faq.a: A debtor established in the Slovak Republic can be sued in a Slovak court under Article 4(1) in conjunction with Article 63(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012. In addition, Article 7(1) allows an action in the courts for the place of performance of the contractual obligation: in the case of the sale of goods, that is the place in a Member State where, under the contract, the goods were delivered or should have been delivered; in the case of services, the place where, under the contract, the services were provided or should have been provided. In the absence of a choice by the parties, the applicable law is determined under Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 593/2008 (Rome I): a contract for the sale of goods is governed by the law of the country where the seller has its habitual residence, and a contract for the provision of services by the law of the country where the service provider has its habitual residence. In an action in Slovakia, the Slovak court therefore generally decides under the law of your state; limitation is then also assessed under that law (Article 12(1)(d)). In such a matter we conduct the proceedings before the Slovak court, and questions of your substantive law we handle with your local counsel there.

faq.q: The debtor claims that the goods were defective. What then?
faq.a: An objection of defects is assessed under the law governing the contract. Where that is Slovak law, the buyer is obliged under Section 427(1) of the Commercial Code to inspect the goods as soon as practicable after the risk of damage to the goods has passed. Under Section 428(1), the buyer’s right arising from defects of the goods cannot be granted in court proceedings if the buyer did not notify the seller of the defects without undue delay after it discovered them or, exercising professional care, ought to have discovered them on inspection; under Section 428(2) that consequence is taken into account only if the seller raises it as an objection in the court proceedings. What matters, therefore, is when and how the customer first notified the defects — we ask for the complaint correspondence among the first documents. In payment order proceedings the statement of opposition must be reasoned on the merits, otherwise the court rejects it (Section 11(1) and Section 12(1)(d) of Act No. 307/2016 Coll.); if the debtor gives reasons for the objection of defects in its statement of opposition, the matter is heard, on the claimant’s application, in ordinary proceedings, where evidence is taken.

faq.q: How long does it take?
faq.a: What we can state are the periods laid down by law. In payment order proceedings the court issues the payment order no later than ten working days after the procedural conditions, including payment of the court fee, are met (Section 7(1) of Act No. 307/2016 Coll.); from service the defendant has 15 days to pay or to file a statement of opposition (Section 7(2)). If one is filed, the claimant is to respond to it and apply for the proceedings to continue within 15 days, and the court then transfers the matter within five working days to the court having jurisdiction under the Civil Contentious Procedure Code (Section 14(1) and (3)). A European order for payment is issued by the court as soon as possible and normally within 30 days of the lodging of the application, and the period for a statement of opposition is 30 days from service (Article 12(1) and Article 16(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006). In enforcement proceedings the court issues the authorisation to carry out enforcement within 15 days of receiving the application, unless there are grounds for dismissing it (Section 53(1) of the Enforcement Code). For ordinary contentious proceedings following a statement of opposition the law lays down no overall period; we therefore do not estimate their length.

faq.q: What if the debtor ends up in bankruptcy in the meantime?
faq.a: Under Section 47(1) of Act No. 7/2005 Coll., the declaration of bankruptcy stays court proceedings concerning assets subject to the bankruptcy, and under Section 48 enforcement proceedings cannot be commenced against those assets; enforcement proceedings already commenced are discontinued upon the declaration of bankruptcy. The claim is then asserted by lodging it in the bankruptcy (Section 28(1)). The basic period for lodging claims is 45 days from the declaration of bankruptcy (Section 28(2)); bankruptcy is declared by publication of the court’s order in the Insolvency Register (Section 23(1)). A claim lodged later is still taken into account, but the creditor cannot exercise the voting right and other rights attached to the lodged claim (Section 28(3)). In restructuring the period is stricter: the claim must be lodged within 30 days of the authorisation of the restructuring, otherwise it is disregarded (Section 121). We therefore check the debtor in the Insolvency Register both before bringing an action and during the proceedings. We cover the lodging of a foreign creditor’s claim in a Slovak bankruptcy on a separate page.

faq.q: Is it worth recovering a small sum as well?
faq.a: That depends on the ratio between the claim, the costs and the debtor’s assets — which is why the matter starts with a check of the debtor and a fee agreed in advance. The following follows from the law: the court fee in payment order proceedings is 3 % of the value of the subject matter, not less than 25 euros; the court awards a party its costs of the proceedings in proportion to its success in the matter (Section 255(1) of the Civil Contentious Procedure Code); and, where Slovak law governs the relationship, the debtor’s default gives rise, alongside default interest, to a right to flat-rate compensation for the costs of recovering the claim in the amount of 40 euros (Section 369c(1) of the Commercial Code and Section 2 of Government Regulation No. 21/2013 Coll.). For claims of up to 5 000 euros there is, in addition, the European Small Claims Procedure under Regulation (EC) No 861/2007: it is a written procedure, representation by a lawyer is not mandatory in it (Article 10), and the unsuccessful party bears the costs of the proceedings, although the court does not award costs that were unnecessarily incurred or are disproportionate to the claim (Article 16). Whether recovery is worthwhile in your matter we state in the assessment, before further costs arise.

faq.q: We already have a judgment or an order for payment from our own state. Can it be enforced in Slovakia?
faq.a: Under Article 39 of Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012, a judgment given in a Member State which is enforceable in that Member State is enforceable in the other Member States without any declaration of enforceability being required. For the purposes of enforcement, Article 42(1) requires a copy of the judgment and the certificate issued by the court of origin under Article 53; under Article 43(1) the certificate is served on the debtor prior to the first enforcement measure. A European order for payment which has become enforceable in the Member State of origin is, under Article 19 of Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006, recognised and enforced in the other Member States without the need for a declaration of enforceability. In Slovakia, a foreign enforcement title enforceable in the Slovak Republic is an enforcement title under Section 45(2)(b) of the Enforcement Code; enforcement is governed by Slovak law, and we file the application for enforcement electronically with the District Court Banská Bystrica.
