faq.q: Do we have to sue again in Slovakia when we already have a judgment from another EU Member State?
faq.a: No. Under Article 36(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012 (Brussels I bis), a judgment given in a Member State is recognised in the other Member States without any special procedure being required, and under Article 39 it is enforceable there without any declaration of enforceability being required. In Slovakia, a foreign enforcement title enforceable in the Slovak Republic is an enforcement title under Section 45(2)(b) of the Enforcement Code; an application for enforcement is filed directly with the District Court Banská Bystrica. The Regulation applies to legal proceedings instituted on or after 10 January 2015 (Article 66(1)); for judgments from earlier proceedings we assess the applicable regime separately.

faq.q: What documents do we need from our own court?
faq.a: For a judgment: a copy of the judgment which satisfies the conditions necessary to establish its authenticity, and the certificate under Article 53 of the Brussels I bis Regulation, which the court of origin issues at the request of any interested party using the form set out in Annex I to the Regulation (Article 42(1)). For a European order for payment: a copy of it as declared enforceable by the court of origin (Article 21(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006); for a European Enforcement Order: a copy of the judgment and a copy of the certificate (Article 20(2) of Regulation (EC) No 805/2004). Under the Enforcement Code, the application is accompanied by a counterpart of the enforcement title with confirmation of enforceability, with which a foreign enforcement title is furnished by the authority of the State in which it was issued (Section 46(1)(c), Section 48(4)(a)) — for a judgment from an EU Member State, enforceability is certified precisely by the certificate under Article 53 (Article 42(1)(b) of the Regulation) — and a foreign legal entity attaches an extract from the register in which it is entered (Section 48(3)(b)).

faq.q: Is a translation into Slovak needed?
faq.a: For a judgment from an EU Member State, not automatically. The competent enforcement authority may, where necessary, require a translation or a transliteration of the contents of the certificate (Article 42(3) of the Brussels I bis Regulation); it may require a translation of the judgment itself only if it is unable to proceed without such a translation (Article 42(4)). The translation is made into Slovak as the official language of the Member State addressed (Article 57(1)) and may be done by a person qualified to do translations in any Member State (Article 57(3)). For a European order for payment, a translation is provided where necessary (Article 21(2)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006). For a foreign arbitral award and the arbitration agreement, an official translation into the Slovak language is always mandatory if they are not drawn up in it (Section 47(2) of Act No. 244/2002 Coll.). Bear in mind also that a debtor domiciled in a Member State other than the Member State of origin may request a translation of the judgment into a language which the debtor understands or into the official language of the Member State in which the debtor is domiciled; until the translation has been provided to the debtor, no measures of enforcement may be taken other than protective measures (Article 43(2)).

faq.q: Can we choose the enforcement officer?
faq.a: No. The enforcement is carried out by the enforcement officer authorised by the court; cases are assigned evenly and at random, using technical and software means, in such a way as to exclude any possibility of influencing the assignment of cases (Section 55(1) of the Enforcement Code). Where the debtor is a legal entity, the case is assigned to an enforcement officer appointed for the territorial district of the regional court in which the debtor has its registered office; for a foreign legal entity, the seat of the organisational unit of its enterprise (organizačná zložka podniku) is decisive (Section 55(2)(b) and (d)). If enforcement in which the court has issued an authorisation is already being conducted against the same debtor, every further case is assigned to the same enforcement officer and the random selection is not used (Section 55(4)).

faq.q: How much does enforcement cost and who pays for it?
faq.a: The court fee for an application for enforcement is 25 euros (item 13(a) of the schedule to Act No. 71/1992 Coll.). The enforcement officer's costs — the fee and reimbursement of expenses — are paid by the debtor, either by satisfying the enforced claim or by having to tolerate their satisfaction out of its assets (Section 199c(4) of the Enforcement Code). Of each payment received, no more than 24 % is applied to the enforcement officer's costs and the remainder to the principal of the enforced claim (Section 60(2)). The creditor is entitled, as against the debtor, to reimbursement of the costs reasonably incurred, to the extent stated by the court in the authorisation to carry out enforcement (Section 199d(1)); these include the expenses of representation in connection with filing the application, the court fee paid and the out-of-pocket expenses connected with filing the application (Section 199a(1)). The lawyer's fee is reimbursed under the provisions on the tariff fee and, up to the commencement of enforcement, at most in the amount of the fee for two acts of legal service (Section 199e). The risk on the creditor's side: if the enforcement officer stops the enforcement, for example because of the debtor's lack of assets, the creditor pays the enforcement officer reimbursement of expenses (Section 199c(1) in conjunction with Section 198(2)).

faq.q: What if the debtor has no assets?
faq.a: The enforcement officer issues a notice stopping the enforcement if, in an enforcement conducted against the assets of a legal entity, no assets or income that could be reached by enforcement and that would be sufficient at least to cover the enforcement officer's costs have been identified within 30 months — in the case of a natural person, within five years — of the commencement of enforcement or of the last occasion on which assets were seized in the enforcement (Section 61n(1)(c) and (d) of the Enforcement Code); these periods are extended by the period for which the enforcement is suspended (Section 61n(7)). In the notice the officer calls on the creditor to pay reimbursement of expenses (Section 61n(3)); a party to the proceedings may file objections with the enforcement officer within 15 days of service (Section 61n(4)). In the case of a commercial company, stopping the enforcement in this way has a further consequence: the notice is published in the Commercial Bulletin (Obchodný vestník) and, upon the expiry of six months from publication, the company is dissolved without liquidation, unless bankruptcy proceedings are pending in respect of it (Section 61n(6)). If bankruptcy has been declared over the debtor's assets, enforcement proceedings against assets subject to the bankruptcy cannot be commenced, and proceedings already commenced are stopped by the declaration of bankruptcy (Section 48 of Act No. 7/2005 Coll.); the claim is then asserted by a proof of claim (prihláška) filed within the basic filing period of 45 days from the declaration of bankruptcy, which a foreign creditor files with the trustee (Section 28(2)). A proof of claim delivered later is taken into account, but the creditor cannot exercise the voting right and other rights attached to the filed claim (Section 28(3)). That is precisely why we check the debtor before the application is filed.

faq.q: We have received a notice of commencement of enforcement and we dispute the claim. What now?
faq.a: The date of service is decisive. Within 15 days of service of the notice you may file with the enforcement officer an application to stop the enforcement, which has suspensive effect; it must state reasons and you must set out in it all the facts that you can rely on as at the date of filing (Section 61k(2) and (5) of the Enforcement Code). The grounds are set out in Section 61k(1) — in particular extinction of the claim after the title came into existence, the setting aside of the title, the inadmissibility of recognition or enforcement of a foreign enforcement title, and other facts which prevent the title from being enforced. Mere disagreement with the claim is not on that list; objections to the claim as such belong in the proceedings from which the title arose — in the case of a payment order, in the statement of opposition. If the court dismisses the application solely because it was filed late, although a ground for stopping the enforcement exists, the debtor is left with an action against the creditor for return of the performance (Section 61l(3)). If the title is a Slovak payment order of which you were unaware, we check how it was served — where it was served abroad, whether the procedure for cross-border service was followed. A Slovak legal entity, for example your subsidiary, is served through its official electronic mailbox, and a document to be served personally on the addressee is deemed served also when the 15-day retention period expires without it having been collected, even if the addressee did not learn of it (Section 32(2) and (5)(b) of Act No. 305/2013 Coll.); an application for a declaration that the electronic service was ineffective must be filed within 15 days of the day on which the addressee became, or could have become, acquainted with the content of the message (Section 33(1) and (2)).

faq.q: We have an arbitral award from a country outside the EU. Can it be enforced in Slovakia?
faq.a: Yes, under the conditions of Act No. 244/2002 Coll. on arbitration, which does not distinguish between an award made in an EU Member State and one made outside the EU: a foreign arbitral award is any arbitral decision on the merits made in the territory of a State other than the Slovak Republic (Section 46(1)). No separate recognition proceedings are needed — the award is recognised by the enforcement court taking it into account as if it were a domestic arbitral award (Section 49(1)). The original or a certified copy of both the award and the arbitration agreement, and their official translation into Slovak, must be attached to the application (Section 47). Before issuing the authorisation, the court serves the award on the debtor, who may within 15 days state grounds precluding recognition or enforcement (Section 54 of the Enforcement Code); recognition and enforcement may be refused only on the grounds set out in Section 50 of the Act. If an application to set aside the arbitral award has been filed in the State of origin, the Slovak court may, on the application of the person who applied for it to be set aside, suspend its enforceability (Section 48).
